operator.name: Northbank Rail
operator.disclaimer: Northbank Rail is a fictional train operating company. All figures in this dataset are synthetic and generated for demonstration purposes.
operator.product: Seat-reserved commuter and regional services. Every ticket carries a specific seat; there is no standing-permitted product.

seatsense.measures: Per-seat occupancy - whether a seat is physically occupied by a person, reported continuously per coach.
seatsense.businessCase: The operator signed off on the rollout against a projected +0.75% of total revenue, from demand-based pricing on measured occupancy alone. No overselling, no reselling of no-show seats, no fare-basket increase.

pilot.scope: 3 units on the Anglia Metro (NBR1), 24 coaches instrumented
findings: Departures that had sold every seat and closed sales departed with an average of 10.4% of those seats empty.
Median 47 paid-for seats travelling empty per sold-out peak departure; worst observed 71.
Ticket data overstated the people on board peak departures by 9-12%.
Two departures the ticket system ranked as equally sold out differed by 5 points of actual occupancy - the no-show rate is a property of who buys that particular train.

demand_classes.label: Morning peak core
demand_classes.description: The 07:00-08:30 arrivals. More people want these than there are seats.

demand_classes.label: Peak shoulder
demand_classes.description: The departures either side of the crush. Where the priced-off demand goes.

demand_classes.label: Off-peak
demand_classes.description: Midday and late evening leisure travel.

demand_classes.label: Evening peak
demand_classes.description: The 16:30-18:00 exodus out of the city. Also demand-constrained.

demand_classes.label: Early / late
demand_classes.description: First and last departures of the day.

sales_policy.reservation: compulsory - every ticket carries a specific seat
sales_policy.basis: A seat reservation is a contractual right to that seat, and denied boarding triggers passenger-rights obligations. European operators therefore sell at most one ticket per seat per departure, unlike airlines, which deliberately overbook and price the denied-boarding risk into their yield model.
consequences: A departure sold to 100% cannot take another passenger. In 2025 the morning peak did exactly that and refused the rest - revenue that never happened.
A seat sold to someone who does not travel departs empty and the revenue is not recoverable: the seat is still theirs, and overselling to cover it is not an option.
Ticket data knows precisely how many seats are unsold. What it cannot know is how many of the sold seats will actually be sat in - so it cannot rank departures by how full they really are.
That ranking is what pricing decisions are made on, which is why measuring it is worth money even though the empty seats themselves are not.
what_seatsense_does_not_do: It does not let the operator oversell. That is a policy and passenger-rights question, not a data question.
It does not let the operator resell a no-show seat mid-journey: the reservation still belongs to its buyer for the whole journey.
It does not reduce the no-show rate. People who have paid still fail to travel at roughly the same rate in 2026 as in 2025.

what_2025_had: Tickets sold and unsold per departure, exactly - one ticket per seat leaves no ambiguity about availability.
Revenue per departure, which is the same whether the ticket holder travels or not.
Whether sales were closed on a departure, and how much demand arrived afterwards.
Gateline entries and exits at staffed stations - a station total, not a seat.
Manual load surveys: a counter with a clicker on a handful of days a year.
what_2025_could_not_have: How many of the sold seats were actually sat in - a no-show is invisible to ticket data.
Therefore the cabin factor of any departure, on any day.
Therefore which of two equally sold-out departures was genuinely full and which was not.
Therefore whether a fare move on a given departure was safe or self-defeating.
ticket_data.reported_metric_2025: assumed_load_factor_pct = tickets sold / seats. Overstates the people on board by the no-show rate.
ticket_data.loadSurveyMethod: Manual count of passengers on board at the busiest point of the journey, morning up services only, plus or minus a few percent counting error. Four days out of 365.

business_case.source: The operator's own projection, signed off before rollout.
business_case.mechanism: Demand-based pricing on measured occupancy. No overselling, no reselling of no-show seats, no increase to the fare basket.
business_case.market_growth_note: Underlying market growth is the counterfactual: what revenue would have done in 2026 without SeatSense-informed pricing. It is generated into the 2026 demand at this rate, so netting it off isolates the pricing effect. Change the parameter to test how sensitive the attribution is.

both_years.tickets_sold: Tickets sold for the departure, never more than the seats there are. A sale, not a person in a seat.
both_years.revenue_gbp: Ticket revenue for the departure. Identical whether the ticket holder travels or not - which is why ticket data cannot see a no-show.
both_years.sales_closed: True if demand exceeded the 100%-of-seats cap and sales were stopped.
both_years.demand_turned_away: Passengers who wanted this departure after sales closed. Not absorbed by overselling, because overselling is not permitted.

2025_only.manual_load_survey: Passengers counted by hand on board, on the four survey days only. The single 2025 field that saw actual people.
2025_only.note: There is no occupancy field for 2025 because no such measurement existed. tickets_sold / seats is an assumed load factor and overstates the people on board by the no-show rate.

2026_only.boarded: People SeatSense saw on board. Tickets sold minus no-shows.
2026_only.seats_occupied: Seats SeatSense measured as physically occupied - the cabin factor numerator. Equal to boarded, since every ticket carries a seat and there is no standing product.
2026_only.ghost_seats: Seats paid for that travelled empty. Not recoverable: the seat still belongs to its buyer and overselling to cover it is not permitted.
2026_only.cf_tickets_sold: Counterfactual: seats this departure would have sold on 2025's pricing rules, with the same market growth applied.
2026_only.cf_revenue_gbp: Counterfactual revenue on the same basis. Observed minus counterfactual is the pricing effect, and that is the SeatSense business case.
